title: What Makes A Ticket Good
eyebrow: Ten faults in how tickets are written, your three answers in, the work started

actions.fyi: All three answers are in and recorded below as D6, D7 and D8. The work is poured and started — override any decision if one reads wrong.

status.now: The audit is done, all ten faults are on the board, and your three answers are recorded. The first of three pieces of work is under way: the board is being taught to refuse a ticket written in words you cannot read.
status.next_up: The board refuses a ticket written in words you cannot read.

items.text: Read every rule that runs when a ticket is written
Measure all nine hundred and fifteen cards against those rules
Prove the weak spots by feeding bad tickets to the checks
File all ten faults as their own cards
The board refuses a ticket written in words you cannot read
Every section of a ticket has to clear a bar a machine can hold
The eighty-eight tickets below the bar swept up to it
Work you sign off carries what good looks like, not just what finished means
Work only your eye can judge always reaches you, and a speed promise always gets measured

content.label: The short version
content.lead: Everything is checked at the end of a job. Almost nothing is checked at the start.

blocks.text: The process around a ticket is immaculate and the ticket itself is uneven.

items: Thirty rules stop a job finishing badly — no reader, no merged change, no real number, no page brought up to date, and it cannot close.
Six rules stop a job starting badly, and four of the six are satisfied by a sentence that means nothing.
So the weakness is entirely at the moment a ticket is written, which is the moment nobody is watching.

content.label: What is checked when a ticket is written
content.lead: Six things. This is the whole list, and what each one actually demands.

rows: What is wrong
Nothing. No length, no shape, no check of any kind
Evidence it is real
Twenty characters of anything
How we know it is done
One digit, or one dot, anywhere in the sentence
Which system, and bug or feature
One of eighteen systems, one of three kinds
Which steps it will run, and why it drops any
Every droppable step taken or refused in writing, twenty-five characters of reason
Who signs it off
You or the agent, and a reason if it is you

blocks.label: I fed the finish-line check some deliberately worthless sentences
blocks.text: 'Done when it feels right, roughly 1 day' is accepted. So is the single character '0'. So is 'e.g. it works'. The check is looking for a digit or a dot to prove a machine could read the sentence, and an opinion with a deadline in it has both.

content.label: What is never checked at all
content.lead: These are the gaps, each now a card.

rows.title: The words a ticket is written in
rows.note: The list of words you cannot read already exists and already guards every page you read. It has never been pointed at the board.

rows.title: What is wrong
rows.note: The one line that names the problem is the only required field with no check whatsoever. A ticket can open on 'fix stuff'.

rows.title: What the ticket is not doing
rows.note: There is a section for it. All 178 tickets carry the same printed sentence in it, so no ticket has ever stated its own edges.

rows.title: How good the result has to be
rows.note: No ticket anywhere says what a good outcome looks like as opposed to a finished one. The agent invents the bar at the end.

rows.title: Whether the ticket itself is any good
rows.note: The reader the board sends is given the change and asked about the code. Nobody has ever re-read the ticket it came from.

rows.title: Subtasks
rows.note: A subtask's finish line has to be eight characters long. That is the entire rule.

rows.title: Anything noticed in passing
rows.note: Filed with no checks at all — not even the twenty characters a real ticket owes.

blocks.label: Two checks that do exist are too narrow to catch the ordinary phrasing
blocks.text: Work only your eye can settle is meant to reach you rather than be signed by the agent — but 'it matches the reference photo', 'the shadows are soft enough' and 'the paint reads as metal to the eye' all slip past and get signed by the agent. Separately, a ticket promising something will be faster must measure it before and after — but 'costs less time on the graphics card', 'cuts the frame budget' and 'cheaper per pixel' are all missed, and the measurement is then dropped without anyone noticing.

content.label: What that has produced across nine hundred and fifteen cards

rows: Tickets with no sections at all
Poured before the shape existed. No evidence, no finish line, nothing
Finish lines no machine can run
'The number exists.' 'It carries a number.' Both passed the check
Finish lines under a hundred characters
Too short to have said anything specific
Subtasks naming no number, file or command
Sixty-two percent. Readable English, but nothing runnable
Tickets whose edges are stated
Every one carries the identical printed sentence
Things noticed in passing that hold up anyway
Nothing forces this. Habit is carrying it, and habit is not a rule

blocks.label: The weak tickets are not scattered — they came in a batch
blocks.text: A hundred and thirty-four of the tickets were poured in bulk from old planning documents. Twenty-eight percent of those have a finish line no machine can run, against thirteen percent of the ones an agent wrote by hand while thinking about the problem. Bulk imports clear a bar; they do not aim above it.

content.label: What a ticket should have to carry
content.lead: Your five sections, with a bar under each that a machine can actually hold.

rows: What is wrong
Written as something observable, not as a fix. Plain words only — every term checked against the same list your report pages are held to. No file names, no run-together names, no shouted initials
Evidence it is real today
Names the thing that proves it: a check that went red and its number, a picture, or your words with the date. A sentence carrying none of the three is refused
How we know it is finished
A command anyone can run and the number or picture it must produce. A digit somewhere in a sentence stops counting
How good it has to be
New. What separates a good result from a merely finished one, and what would make it a no. Required on anything you sign off yourself
What this is not doing
Written per ticket or the ticket is refused. The printed sentence stops being accepted as an answer
Subtasks
Each one held to the same bar as the finish line above it — a command and its number, not eight characters of anything

blocks.label: None of this needs a new tool
blocks.text: The shape of a ticket, the word list, and the machine that refuses a bad one all exist already. Every fault here is a check that was never written or was written too loosely, in one place that every ticket already passes through.

decisions.title: The ten faults were filed as cards rather than listed here
decisions.why: A finding in a document is a finding nobody will do. Each is now on the board with the evidence attached, so your three answers turn straight into work.

decisions.title: Unreadable titles get a rule, not a rewrite
decisions.why: Your instruction. I had started rewriting the nine cards I filed by hand and stopped — six are in plain words and three are not, and the rule will sweep the rest. Hand-fixing leaves the next agent free to do it again.

decisions.title: Subtasks are held to the same bar as the ticket above them
decisions.why: The ticket demands a runnable finish line and its subtasks demand eight characters, so the work is checked hardest where the least of it happens.

decisions.title: No new kind of ticket — the standard goes on the shape that exists
decisions.why: One shape, poured one way, checked in one place. A second kind would need its own checks and would drift from the first within a month.

decisions.title: Refusals name the fix, not just the fault
decisions.why: Every refusal on this board already reads as a sentence telling you what to do instead, and that is why they get followed rather than worked around.

decisions.title: A ticket written in words you cannot read is refused, not warned about
decisions.why: Your answer. The word list that already guards every page you read gets pointed at the board, and a ticket carrying one of those words is turned away naming the plain word to use instead.

decisions.title: What good looks like is required only on work you sign off yourself
decisions.why: Your answer. It becomes a required section exactly when a ticket is opened as yours to judge, and stays optional on the plumbing nobody looks at.

decisions.title: The eighty-eight are swept now, and the checker is built first so there is a bar to sweep to
decisions.why: Your answer was to sweep before anything else. The bar a sweep aims at is the checker itself, so it is built first — hours, not a day — and then the same machine that will refuse the next bad ticket verifies all eighty-eight. Sweeping first would mean rewriting eighty-eight tickets against an agent's guess at the standard.

decisions.title: Three pieces of work, not ten
decisions.why: The ten faults collapse onto one moment: when a ticket is written. Two of the three pieces change that moment; the third is the sweep. The rest are filed and wait behind them.

next.if_nothing: The three pieces run in the order below, and you next hear from me when the eighty-eight are swept.
